explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Luke says the chief priests and scribes were looking for a way to put Jesus to death, "…for they feared the people." Looking for a way tells me they hadn't found one yet.

The Romans, the empire's soldiers and officials, are a fair guess, baker. But verse 2 doesn't say a word about them. It says the chief priests and scribes feared the people. Sometimes the answer is sitting right there in the verse.

The Pharisees are another group of religious leaders who show up around Jesus in the Gospels (Luke 5:30), so I see why that one came to mind. Here, though, verse 2 only names the chief priests and scribes, and it says they feared the people. I think it's a good reminder to check who the verse actually names before you pick.

explanations.answer: The chief priests and temple officers
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Verse 4 says Judas went to discuss it with the chief priests and temple officers. Verse 2 says the chief priests were already looking for a way to put Jesus to death.

Pilate was the Roman governor (Luke 3:1), so I get why you'd think of him. But in this passage Judas doesn't go to Pilate or any soldiers. Verse 4 says he went to the chief priests and temple officers. Pilate's name isn't in these verses at all.

Herod was the ruler of Galilee (Luke 3:1), and that name does pop up in the Gospels. It just doesn't pop up here, friend. Luke 22:4 says Judas went to the chief priests and temple officers. That's the whole guest list.
Right, baker. Verse 5 says the chief priests and officers "…were delighted and agreed to give him money." So the money was part of the deal. It's a heavy moment, and the text doesn't dress it up.

Close, but it's the other way around, friend. Luke 22:5 says the chief priests and officers were delighted and agreed to give Judas money. So the money is right there in the deal. It's a heavy part of the story, and the text says it plainly.

That's right, baker. Verse 6 says Judas looked for an opportunity to betray Jesus "…in the absence of a crowd." He agreed to the deal and then he started watching for the right time. The text doesn't say why a crowd mattered to him, so I'll leave that open.

explanations.answer: One in front of the whole temple
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite, friend. Verse 6 says Judas looked for an opportunity "…in the absence of a crowd." A packed temple is about as far from that as you can get. It's like waiting for a quiet moment and picking the loudest room in town.

Jesus does teach at the temple (Luke 21:37), so I see why that came to mind. But verse 6 says Judas looked for an opportunity "…in the absence of a crowd." Teaching isn't what the verse names. The moment he's after is one with no crowd.
Yes, baker. Peter, one of Jesus's disciples (Luke 6:14), is named in verse 8. Jesus sends him to make the preparations for the Passover. He's one half of the pair.
That's right, friend. John, another of Jesus's disciples (Luke 6:14), is the second name in verse 8. Jesus sends him along with Peter to prepare the Passover. Two names, one errand.
James was one of Jesus's disciples too (Luke 6:14), so he's in the right crowd. But verse 8 says Jesus sent Peter and John. James isn't named for this errand.
Andrew was also one of Jesus's disciples (Luke 6:14), so I see the thinking, baker. Verse 8 names Peter and John for this job, though. Andrew isn't mentioned in these preparations.
Thomas is on the list of Jesus's disciples too (Luke 6:15), so he's in the right company, baker. Verse 8 has Jesus sending Peter and John, though. Those are the two names Luke gives for this errand.

explanations.answer: He'll be carrying a jug of water
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Jesus says, "…a man carrying a jug of water will meet you." That's the whole clue for Peter and John to look for. Think of it as a landmark that walks.

explanations.answer: He'll be leading a young donkey
explanations.explanation: A young animal does come up when Jesus sends disciples on another errand, where they find a colt tied up (Luke 19:30). That's a different trip, though, friend. Here in verse 10 the man is "…carrying a jug of water…" No animal involved.

explanations.answer: He'll be holding a lit lamp
explanations.explanation: A lamp is a nice picture, baker, but it isn't in the verse. Jesus says the man will be "…carrying a jug of water…" That's the sign for Peter and John to watch for. A lit lamp isn't mentioned anywhere in this passage.

explanations.answer: A large upper room already furnished
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Jesus says the owner "…will show you a large upper room, already furnished." Then He tells them, "Make preparations there." Large, upstairs and furnished, all in one verse.

explanations.answer: A small room off the courtyard
explanations.explanation: Close on the room, baker, but small is the one word that doesn't fit. Jesus says the owner will show them "…a large upper room, already furnished." A courtyard isn't in the verse at all, and neither is small.

explanations.answer: A space up on the flat roof
explanations.explanation: Up is right, friend, but a roof isn't what Jesus says. Verse 12 says "…a large upper room, already furnished." It's a room, and it's already furnished. No roof in sight.
It's the other way around, baker. Verse 13 says they went and found it "…just as Jesus had told them." So what they found matched what Jesus had said. That's the opposite of a twist.
Right, friend. Luke 22:13 says Peter and John went and found it "…just as Jesus had told them." Then they prepared the Passover. Everything matched what Jesus said.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, "I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before My suffering." He's the one who wants this meal, and He says it out loud. I think that's worth leaning in close for.

The Sabbath is a real thing in the Gospels (Luke 6:1), friend, but it isn't in what Jesus says here. Verse 15 says He has eagerly desired to eat this Passover with them "…before My suffering." That's the one thing He names.

Crowds do come up in this passage, baker, but not in this sentence. Jesus says, "I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before My suffering." The word is suffering. Nothing about a crowd in that verse.

It's the opposite, friend. Jesus says, "For I tell you that I will not drink of the fruit of the vine from now on until the kingdom of God comes." So He's not promising to keep drinking it every Passover. He points ahead to the kingdom of God coming.

Right, baker. Jesus says, "For I tell you that I will not drink of the fruit of the vine from now on until the kingdom of God comes." He's not promising to keep drinking it Passover after Passover. He points ahead to the kingdom of God coming.
You got it, baker. Jesus picks up the bread, gives thanks, breaks it and passes it to His apostles. He says it is His body, given for them. Then He asks them to keep doing this to remember Him.

Manna was real bread from heaven (Exodus 16:4), baker. God fed Israel with it in the wilderness for forty years (Exodus 16:35). But Jesus doesn't call this bread manna. He says, "This is My body, given for you…"

Temple officers show up earlier in this passage, friend, but Jesus doesn't bring up the temple here. He gives thanks, breaks the bread and says, "This is My body, given for you…" That's how He describes it.
That's the one, friend. Jesus says, "do this in remembrance of Me." It's an invitation to remember Him. Simple words, and I'd write them on every cookie box if I could.
Jesus does give commands in other places, baker, but that isn't the word here. In verse 19 He says, "do this in remembrance of Me." The word is remembrance. It's about remembering Him.
Nobody's being handed a shield here, friend. Jesus says, "do this in remembrance of Me." The word is remembrance, and the verse doesn't mention defending anyone. It's all about remembering Him.

explanations.answer: The new covenant in His blood poured out for them
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, "This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you." He says it after supper, with the cup in His hands. It's a big sentence, so read it slowly.

explanations.answer: A reminder of their rescue out of Egypt
explanations.explanation: The Passover itself looks back to Egypt, where the LORD passed over the houses of the Israelites (Exodus 12:27). I see why that came to mind, friend. But in Luke 22:20 Jesus says something else about the cup: "This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you."

explanations.answer: A blessing on the owner of this house
explanations.explanation: The owner of the house does matter in this story, since he provides the room. But Jesus doesn't say anything about blessing him over this cup. Verse 20 says, "This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you." The cup is about the new covenant.
It's the other way around, friend. Jesus says, "Look! The hand of My betrayer is with Mine on the table." So the betrayer is at the table, close enough to reach. I think this one hurts to read.
Right, baker. Luke 22:21 has Jesus say, "Look! The hand of My betrayer is with Mine on the table." So the betrayer isn't far away. He's at the table with them. It's a heavy moment.

Not quite, friend. Verse 23 says they "…began to question among themselves which of them was going to do this." If they all knew right away, there'd be nothing to question. They were asking each other.

You got it, baker. Luke 22:23 says they began to question among themselves which of them was going to do this. I think that means it wasn't plain to them right away. The text doesn't say more than that.
